result.question:
CI/CD best practices, patterns, and anti-patterns (2024-2026) for a large Rust monorepo built with Buck2 and gated by GitHub Actions, migrating toward an owned/self-hosted CI/CD control plane (Prow + Tekton + Argo class). Synthesize with citations, focused on THREE founder pillars plus rollout:

(1) THROUGHPUT optimization — affected-target/incremental builds (Buck2/Bazel remote build execution + remote caching), merge queues / change batching, presubmit-vs-postsubmit split, test sharding & parallelism, monorepo CI scaling (Google TAP/Meta/Uber SubmitQueue patterns), and how to keep wall-clock low at scale.

(2) SURFACE-ALL-ISSUES vs FAIL-FAST — how leading orgs run ALL checks to completion and aggregate EVERY failure into one report so a developer fixes everything in a single sweep: non-fail-fast CI matrices, GitHub Actions problem-matchers/annotations, aggregated check-run summaries, collect-all-then-report test runners, continue-on-error semantics. Explain the tradeoff against fast-feedback and how to get BOTH via parallelism (fan-out all checks concurrently, none short-circuits, aggregate at join).

(3) ANTI-PATTERNS to avoid — flaky-test tolerance, false-green / non-blocking 'required' checks, fail-fast hiding downstream errors, serial pipelines, unpinned/non-reproducible builds, manual gates that drift, and self-approval.

(4) ROLLOUT — required-status-check & branch-protection best practice, signed commits, and the gradual rollout of a NEW required gate (shadow → required) WITHOUT blocking every merge (baseline/ratchet 'block-on-new' patterns), plus the GitHub-Actions → owned Prow/Tekton/Argo migration pattern and how to run a new control plane in shadow before cutover.

Deliver: concrete recommendations for our stack, an explicit best-practice-vs-anti-pattern table, the throughput techniques ranked by ROI, the surface-all-without-sacrificing-throughput design, and citations.
result.summary: For a large Rust monorepo on Buck2 gated by GitHub Actions and migrating toward an owned Prow/Tekton/Argo control plane, the verified evidence converges on a clear playbook. THROUGHPUT at scale comes from affected-target/incremental builds driven by a reverse build-dependency graph (Google TAP runs only AFFECTED targets, not the full pool; Buck2 speaks Bazel's Remote Execution API so it can use EngFlow/BuildBarn/BuildBuddy for remote build execution and caching), a presubmit-vs-postsubmit split (fast/reliable tests gate merges, comprehensive tests run postsubmit), and a speculative merge queue (Uber SubmitQueue, which cut CI resource use 53% / CPU 44% / p95 wait 37% in 2024). SURFACE-ALL-ISSUES without sacrificing speed is achieved by fanning out all checks concurrently with none short-circuiting and aggregating at the join: cargo-nextest's --failure-output=final/immediate-final and JUnit XML output, dorny/test-reporter glob-aggregating sharded results into one Check Run + Job Summary, and GitHub Actions problem matchers turning tool output into inline annotations. The dominant ANTI-PATTERNS the evidence warns against are flaky-test tolerance (Google: ~1.5% of all test RUNS flake, and ~16% of tests are ever flaky) and treating per-commit full-suite testing as viable (compute grows quadratically). ROLLOUT best practice is data-driven: because ~91% of affected tests never fail and the per-change pass:fail ratio is ~99:1, you can relocate exhaustiveness to postsubmit, run new gates in shadow first, and use speculative batching so one bad change never blocks the batch.

findings.claim: PILLAR 1 (THROUGHPUT) — Affected-target/incremental builds are the foundational throughput lever. Compute the minimal set of targets/tests to run per change from a reverse build-dependency graph rather than running the full suite each time. Google TAP derives AFFECTED test targets by hashing BUILD-rule dependencies on changed source files; bazel-diff implements the same idea by SHA256-hashing the full build graph at two revisions and diffing. RECOMMENDATION for our stack: use Buck2's native target-determinator / change-detector for affected-target selection (bazel-diff is Bazel-specific and a fallback pattern, not Buck2-native).
findings.evidence: Merges claims [1], [10], [14], [15]. SWE@Google ch23: 'The primary mechanism for determining which tests need to be run is an analysis of the downstream dependency graph for every change.' TAP paper (Memon/Gao, ICSE-SEIP 2017): TAP 'uses build dependencies in the BUILD files ... to create a reverse dependency structure that ... outputs all test targets that ... depend on the modified files; these are called AFFECTED test targets.' bazel-diff (Tinder): generate-hashes produces a SHA256 hashmap of the entire Bazel graph at each revision; diffing the two JSON files yields the impacted target set. Each target's hash is content-addressed over rule implementation + every attribute + all rule_inputs + source-file content SHA256, so any direct or transitive change flips the hash. CAVEAT: bazel-diff is Bazel-specific; for Buck2 use buck2's own target-determinator. Hash-based selection can occasionally over- or under-include (e.g., comment-only changes flip the hash), so empirically validate the impact set.

findings.claim: PILLAR 1 (THROUGHPUT) — Remote build execution + remote caching is vendor-portable for Buck2 because Buck2 implements Bazel's Remote Execution API standard. RECOMMENDATION: connect the Buck2 monorepo to any RE-API-conformant service; concrete, production-tested options are EngFlow, BuildBarn, and BuildBuddy. This gives distributed execution and a shared cache so unchanged targets are never rebuilt and work fans out across a farm.
findings.evidence: Merges claims [8], [9]. Official Buck2 docs: 'Buck2 can use services that expose Bazel's remote execution API' and 'Buck2 projects have been successfully tested for remote execution against EngFlow, BuildBarn and BuildBuddy.' The facebook/buck2 repo ships runnable configs under examples/remote_execution/ (buildbarn, buildbuddy, engflow, nativelink). CAVEATS (do not refute interoperability): Buck2 does NOT implement Bazel's Build Event Stream, its RE client is less configurable than Bazel's, and there are per-backend symlink/asset-digest quirks plus a UNAVAILABLE-retry workaround; the open-source RE binding is 'less polished' than Meta's internal one. The word 'any' is a slight overreach — read it as 'any RE-API-conformant service, modulo per-backend quirks.'

findings.claim: PILLAR 1 (THROUGHPUT) — Split CI into presubmit (only fast, reliable tests, accepting some coverage loss to keep wall-clock low) and postsubmit (comprehensive, longer, less-stable tests), explicitly trading presubmit exhaustiveness for throughput and catching the small fraction of issues that slip through on postsubmit. Running the entire suite on every submission does not scale; removing the presubmit-must-be-exhaustive constraint yields large efficiency gains.
findings.evidence: Merges claims [2], [3]. SWE@Google ch23: presubmit runs 'only fast, reliable ones'; 'You can accept some loss of coverage on presubmit, but that means you need to catch any issues that slip by on post-submit, and accept some number of rollbacks.' Also: 'waiting a long time to run every test during code submission can be severely disruptive. Further, by removing the constraint for presubmits to be exhaustive, a lot of efficiency gains can be made' — explicitly conditioned on running a comprehensive postsubmit suite. RECOMMENDATION for our stack: presubmit = affected unit/small tests + lint/typecheck via Buck2 affected-targets; postsubmit = full affected + integration + slow tests asynchronously, with rollback automation.

findings.claim: PILLAR 1 (THROUGHPUT) — A speculative merge queue is the canonical change-batching pattern for keeping trunk green at high merge volume. Uber SubmitQueue speculatively rebases and validates multiple changes in PARALLEL against predicted future states of HEAD (a pruned speculation tree of all possible builds), lands only changes whose builds succeed, and on failure isolates the offending change and auto-retries the rest with no human intervention — so one bad change never blocks the batch. The original EuroSys 2019 work reduced master breakage from 50% to 0%; the July 2024 strategy rollout across Go/iOS/Android cut CI resource usage ~53%, weekly CPU hours ~44%, and p95 wait ~37%.
findings.evidence: Merges claims [4], [5], [6], [7]. uber/submitqueue README: 'a high-performance speculative merge queue ... speculatively rebases and validates multiple changes in parallel against predicted future states of HEAD'; 'When they fail, SubmitQueue isolates the offending change and retries the rest — all without human intervention.' arXiv 2501.03440 (ICSE-SEIP 2025, Uber): 'speculatively executes builds and only lands changes with successful outcomes ... constructing a speculation tree that outlines all possible builds'; 'On July 22nd, 2024, we rolled out a new strategy across three of Uber's largest monorepos—Go, iOS, and Android' with '~53% [CI resource], 44% [CPU], 37% [P95 wait]' reductions (aggregate across the three repos; per-repo figures vary). EuroSys 2019 'Keeping Master Green at Scale' is the peer-reviewed basis. RECOMMENDATION: adopt a merge queue (GitHub merge queue today; SubmitQueue-style speculation in the owned control plane) so the cost of serial validation (last change waits days at 1000 changes/day x 30 min) is eliminated.

findings.claim: PILLAR 1 (THROUGHPUT) — Proof points that monorepo CI scaling works at extreme volume, justifying the affected-target + batching architecture: Google TAP gates nearly all changes, handling >50,000 unique changes/day and >4 billion test cases/day; on an average day it integrates/tests >13K projects requiring 800K builds and 150M test runs over a ~2B-LOC monolith with a commit roughly every second. Per-commit testing is not cost-effective because compute grows quadratically (submission rate x test-pool size, each linear), so TAP batches commits into 'milestone' epochs cut ~every 45 minutes at peak.
findings.evidence: Merges claims [0], [11], [12]. SWE@Google ch23: '...handling more than 50,000 unique changes and running more than four billion individual test cases' and TAP 'is the gateway for almost all changes at Google.' TAP paper: 'In an average day, TAP integrates and tests ... more than 13K code projects, requiring 800K builds and 150 Million test runs' over a '2 Billion LOC codebase—structured largely as a single monolithic code tree' with 'a code commit every second on the average'; 'the compute resources were growing quadratically with two multiplicative linear factors' so 'A milestone is typically cut every 45 minutes during peak.' CAVEAT: figures are circa 2016-2019 (historical lower bounds illustrating scale), not live 2026 metrics. RELEVANCE: validates milestone-batching as a throughput lever where merge volume makes per-commit testing prohibitive.

findings.claim: PILLAR 2 (SURFACE-ALL-ISSUES vs FAIL-FAST) — Get BOTH fast feedback and a complete failure report by fanning out all checks concurrently with none short-circuiting, then aggregating at the join. For Rust tests, cargo-nextest's --failure-output=final defers each failing test's stdout/stderr to the end so all failures are aggregated together (default is immediate; nextest recommends immediate-final for CI — print immediately AND re-summarize at the end). RECOMMENDATION: run nextest with a non-fail-fast profile and immediate-final output so the developer sees a single consolidated list of every failure per run.
findings.evidence: Claim [16]. nextest docs: '--failure-output — When to display standard output and standard error for failing tests. The default is immediate. ... final — Display output at the end of the test run.' Docs further recommend 'immediate-final' as 'most useful for CI jobs.' This is the collect-all-then-report runner behavior the research question asks for: no short-circuit on first failure, all failure output emitted together at the join.

findings.claim: PILLAR 2 (SURFACE-ALL-ISSUES) — Aggregate EVERY result into one machine-readable report and one PR-visible summary. cargo-nextest emits JUnit/XUnit XML (one consolidated report per profile, e.g. target/nextest/ci/junit.xml). dorny/test-reporter then glob-aggregates result files across parallel/sharded jobs (comma-separated, fast-glob wildcard paths; all files must share one format) into a SINGLE GitHub Check Run plus an Actions Job Summary, annotates the exact failing code location from the captured message/stack trace, and lets you list all/failed/none test cases — the surface-all pattern rather than fail-fast. It collects all results before optionally failing the run via fail-on-error.
findings.evidence: Merges claims [17], [18], [19]. nextest: 'Nextest can produce output in the JUnit/XUnit XML format. This format is widely understood by test analysis tools and libraries.' dorny/test-reporter action.yml: path is a 'Comma-separated list of paths to test results. Supports wildcards via fast-glob. All matched result files must be of same format'; it 'Annotates code where it failed based on message and stack trace captured during test execution'; list-tests = all/failed/none. The Actions Summary 'will contain a table listing each test results file and the number of passed, failed, and skipped tests' — i.e. aggregates sharded jobs into one report. CAVEATS: inline annotations capped by max-annotations (<=50, default 10) and nextest follows the Jenkins JUnit variant (some readers may need post-processing); skipped tests not always emitted (nextest issue #885).

findings.claim: PILLAR 2 (SURFACE-ALL-ISSUES) — Use GitHub Actions problem matchers to surface non-test tool failures (rustc, clippy, fmt, build errors) as inline annotations so EVERY issue across the fan-out lands in the PR UI. A problem matcher scans an action's log output for a configured regex and produces BOTH GitHub Annotations and log-file decorations on match. Regex captures map to named fields file, line, column, message, code, and severity (severity accepts 'warning' or 'error', case-insensitive, default error), letting failures be tagged and aggregated as inline annotations.
findings.evidence: Merges claims [20], [21]. actions/toolkit docs: 'Problem Matchers are a way to scan the output of actions for a specified regex pattern and surface that information prominently in the UI. ... Both GitHub Annotations and log file decorations are created when a match is detected.' Field list: file, line, column, severity ('either warning or error case-insensitive. Defaults to error'), code, message. CAVEAT: annotations are capped (10 each warning/error/notice per step, 50 per job, 50 per run), so a problem matcher does not literally render every failure inline beyond the cap — pair with a full aggregated summary report (see test-reporter finding).

findings.claim: PILLAR 3 (ANTI-PATTERNS) — Flaky-test tolerance is the headline anti-pattern: flakiness is large-scale and corrosive even at a world-class org. Google measured ~1.5% of ALL test RUNS reporting a flaky result (a test that passes and fails on the same code) and ~16% of tests (more than 1 in 7) exhibiting some flakiness. RECOMMENDATION: never tolerate flaky 'required' checks — quarantine/auto-detect flakes (nextest retry+quarantine, flake databases), keep them OUT of the blocking presubmit gate, and treat false-green as a defect, because flaky required checks both block good changes and erode trust in the gate.
findings.evidence: Merges claims [22], [23]. Google Testing Blog (Micco, 2016): 'across our entire corpus of tests, we see a continual rate of about 1.5% of all test runs reporting a flaky result. We define a flaky test result as a test that exhibits both a passing and a failing result with the same code.' And: 'Almost 16% of our tests have some level of flakiness ... more than 1 in 7 of the tests ... occasionally fail in a way not caused by changes to the code or tests.' CAVEAT: figures are from 2016 (historical, self-reported snapshot), not current rates — cite as evidence that flakiness is structurally large at scale, not as a 2026 metric.

findings.claim: PILLAR 4 (ROLLOUT) — The empirical foundation for a baseline/ratchet 'block-on-new' rollout: most affected tests almost never fail, so you can introduce new gates without blocking every merge. Of 5.5M affected test targets over one month, only 63K ever failed; 91.3% passed at least once and never failed; the per-change PASSED:FAILED ratio is ~99:1. RECOMMENDATION: run a NEW required gate in SHADOW (non-blocking, continue-on-error, report-only) first, ratchet to block-on-NEW-failures against a recorded baseline, and only then make it a hard required status check — exactly the pattern Google uses to de-prioritize near-always-passing tests and reduce turnaround.
findings.evidence: Claim [13]. TAP paper: 'of the 5.5 Million affected tests that we analyzed for a time period, only 63K ever failed ... 91.3% PASSED at least once and never FAILED ... the ratio of PASSED vs. FAILED test targets per code change is 99:1, which means that test turnaround time may be significantly reduced if tests that almost never FAIL, when affected, are re-executed less frequently.' This 99:1 ratio is the quantitative justification for (a) shadow-first rollout of new gates and (b) frequency-reducing / de-prioritizing stable tests. Maps directly to the founder's gradual-rollout (shadow -> required) and baseline/ratchet requirements.

result.caveats: TIME-SENSITIVITY: Google TAP scale figures (50K changes/day, 4B test cases, 13K projects, 800K builds, 150M runs, ~2B LOC, commit/sec) are circa 2016-2019 and should be cited as historical lower bounds illustrating monorepo CI scale, not live 2026 metrics. Likewise the flaky-test numbers (1.5% of runs; 16% of tests) are from a 2016 Google blog post — strong primary evidence that flakiness is structurally large at scale, but a dated snapshot, not a current rate. STACK-SPECIFIC GAP: bazel-diff (claims [14],[15]) is Bazel-specific, not Buck2-native — the affected-target MECHANISM transfers directly, but for a Buck2 monorepo you should use Buck2's own target-determinator/change-detector rather than bazel-diff. BUCK2 RE LIMITATIONS: Buck2 implements Bazel's Remote Execution API but NOT the Build Event Stream, its RE client is less configurable than Bazel's, and there are per-backend (EngFlow/BuildBarn/BuildBuddy) symlink/asset-digest quirks plus a UNAVAILABLE-retry workaround; the open-source RE binding is less polished than Meta's internal one. The 'any RE service' phrasing is a mild overreach (read: any RE-API-conformant service, modulo quirks). SURFACE-ALL TOOLING CAPS: GitHub inline annotations are capped (10/step, 50/job, 50/run) and dorny/test-reporter max-annotations defaults to 10 (<=50), so inline annotation is NOT a complete surface-all channel by itself — it must be paired with a full aggregated JUnit/summary report. nextest follows the Jenkins JUnit XML variant and may not emit skipped tests (issue #885). EVIDENCE-COVERAGE GAPS NOT in the verified claim set (treat as not-yet-evidenced rather than recommended): the verified claims do NOT cover the GitHub Actions -> Prow/Tekton/Argo migration mechanics, branch-protection/required-status-check configuration specifics, signed-commit enforcement, or running a new control plane in shadow before cutover. The rollout finding [13] supports shadow->required gating in principle (via the 99:1 stable-test ratio), but the control-plane-migration and signed-commit pillars (4) were not substantiated by surviving claims. One claim was REFUTED (3-0 against): cargo-nextest's --final-status-level default is NOT 'fail' as originally asserted — do not rely on that; use the verified --failure-output=immediate-final mechanism instead.
openQuestions: What is the concrete GitHub Actions -> owned Prow/Tekton/Argo migration pattern, and how do you run the new control plane in shadow (mirroring presubmits) before cutover? No surviving claim addressed this pillar.

What are the specific branch-protection / required-status-check settings and signed-commit (e.g. Sigstore/gitsign, GPG, or Gitea/GitHub commit-signing) enforcement steps for the rollout pillar? Not covered by verified evidence.

Does Buck2's native target-determinator / change-detector match bazel-diff's accuracy and over/under-inclusion behavior in practice for a large Rust monorepo, and what is the recommended way to validate its impact set empirically?
What are current (2024-2026) flaky-test rates and quarantine/auto-retry effectiveness benchmarks, given the only verified flakiness figures are Google's 2016 snapshot?

refuted.claim: cargo-nextest's --final-status-level option controls which test statuses are displayed at the end of a test run, and its default value is 'fail', meaning all failing tests are listed in a summary at the end of the run (a surface-all-failures aggregation behavior).
